title: Corrosion Costs India 4.3% of GDP Every Year, Report Finds
excerpt: Nomura Research Institute puts the annual loss at Rs 14.15 lakh crore and says lifecycle costing and tougher standards could recover 1.5% of GDP.
body:
• Corrosion costs India an estimated Rs 14.15 lakh crore a year, or 4.3% of GDP, above the global average of 3.4%, according to a Nomura Research Institute report.
  • Power generation and transmission is hit hardest, losing 10.1% of sectoral GDP; railways lose about $3 billion a year and infrastructure alone loses Rs 1.42 lakh crore.
  • Better corrosion management could add about 1.5% to GDP, roughly Rs 5 trillion a year, the report estimates.
  • For builders and buyers: the fix starts at purchase — tenders and contracts judged on lifetime cost, not lowest upfront price, and exposure-based standards for coastal and high-humidity sites.

India loses an estimated 4.3% of its gross domestic product to corrosion every year. The figure, from a report by Nomura Research Institute (NRI), puts the annual loss at around Rs 14.1 trillion. Rust is a recurring charge on highways, bridges, railways, power networks, telecom towers, buildings and factories, paid in premature repairs, replacements and lost productivity.

The loss is larger than the global average of 3.4% of GDP. The report links India's higher burden to its long coastline, high humidity, industrial pollution and sharply different exposure conditions from one region to another — differences that uniform project specifications still largely ignore.

Where the money is lost

Power generation and transmission carries the highest corrosion intensity, with losses estimated at 10.1% of sectoral GDP. Telecommunications loses 3.8% of sectoral GDP, automobiles 3.0% and railways 2.8%, according to a summary of the report in Coatings Journal. Railways alone lose an estimated $3 billion a year. India has more than 8.13 lakh telecom towers supporting 2.948 million base transceiver stations, a steel-intensive network exposed to weather across the country.

Infrastructure bears the largest absolute burden. A CII-NRI presentation of the findings in New Delhi in September put the infrastructure sector's annual corrosion loss at Rs 1.42 lakh crore, equal to 2.9% of the sector's GDP, as reported by Odisha Stand. The report cited bridge failures, including the Andheri bridge collapse and the CSMT foot-over bridge incident in Mumbai, as examples of what premature deterioration can cost beyond repair bills.

Why upfront-cheapest keeps losing

The report's central argument is about how India buys. Public tenders that reward the lowest upfront construction cost can lock in decades of repainting, repair and early replacement. The NRI recommendations start with shifting public infrastructure tendering to lifecycle cost analysis, so a bid is judged on the cost of owning and maintaining the asset over its life, not only on the cost of building it.

The infrastructure presentation gave a concrete comparison. Multi-coat paint can look cheaper at purchase, but its lifetime expense is nearly double because it must be reapplied repeatedly. Hot-dip galvanizing costs about 10% more upfront and can provide more than 100 years of maintenance-free protection in highly corrosive environments, the report said. On a lifetime basis, the apparently expensive option is the cheap one.

The standards gap

The second fix is regulatory. The report calls for strengthening Bureau of Indian Standards rules to align with global durability practice, adding exposure-based durability requirements, and mandating stronger corrosion protection for steel-intensive sectors such as telecom, transport and public infrastructure. In the United States and Japan, exposure-based protection is mandatory. In India, the report noted, such measures are still largely optional.

It also recommends modern testing methods, including magnetic gauge and eddy-current techniques, clearer specifications for coating thickness and repair limits, stricter inspection and maintenance protocols for long-life assets, and wider use of corrosion-resistant materials in harsh environments, including renewable energy installations.

What changes if India acts

The prize is large. Adopting stronger corrosion-management practices could improve GDP by about 1.5%, or roughly Rs 5 trillion a year, through longer asset life and lower lifecycle costs, the report estimates. For infrastructure alone, achievable savings were put at Rs 49,580 crore a year. The timing matters because India is in the middle of a large build-out of roads, railways, housing, airports, ports and renewable capacity. Every asset built now to a weak durability standard carries its corrosion bill forward for decades.

The report frames corrosion as an economic and policy issue, not only an engineering one. That framing points to the next steps: whether lifecycle costing enters central and state tender rules, whether exposure-based standards become mandatory for coastal and industrial zones, and whether inspection data starts to be collected asset by asset. Until those rules change, the 4.3% figure is best read as a standing annual cost, not a one-off finding.
